Laocoon. A prominent Trojan priest, either serving Apollo or Poseidon depending on which tradition you follow, he is remembered for his famous warning to the city. When the Greeks presented Troy with an enormous wooden horse, claiming it as an offering to the gods, Laocoon alone recognized the danger. He pleaded with King Priam to reject the horse, speaking the words that would echo through history: I fear the Greeks, even bearing gifts. His warnings fell on deaf ears, as the Trojans were convinced the horse was safe, or perhaps deceived by the gods themselves. For his defiance, Laocoon was punished by divine wrath. Giant sea serpents were sent to attack him, and he was strangled to death along with his two sons in view of all Troy. The Aeneid presents his death as divine retribution for his presumption or for his role in the war itself. The statue depicting Laocoon and his sons wrestling with the serpents became one of antiquity's most famous works of art, immortalizing the moment of his death and serving as a symbol of fate and divine wrath that mortals could not escape.
